title: Finders Keepers: Real Law
summary: Josh and Chuck explore "finders keepers" law: how found property is handled in the US and UK, starting with the John and Mary saddle ridge gold coin hoard in California. They cover treasure law, the distinction between lost, mislaid, and abandoned property, a Texas-style private property argument over cash hidden in an Arizona house, a Georgia public defender who pocketed a diamond ring found at a Target, and undersea shipwreck treasure disputes including the San Jose galleon off Colombia, the Notre Dame de Deliverance off Florida, the Abandoned Shipwreck Act, and Tommy Thompson's S.S. Central America case. The episode closes with listener mail from a cognitive psychologist about the Stanford prison experiment episode.
topics: gold coin treasure found on property

segments.title: Opening banter on finders keepers
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the finders keepers and losers weepers idea and their shared sense that finders should not keep other people's property.

segments.title: Saddle Ridge gold coin hoard
segments.summary: A California couple, John and Mary (pseudonyms), found eight cans of rare gold coins buried on their land, possibly worth up to ten million dollars. They discuss how the land ownership and the age of the coins strengthen their claim, and how US finders law varies by state and court.
topics: gold coin treasure found on property
US found property law varies by state

segments.title: Treasure law and UK approach
segments.summary: They explain that old gold coins count as treasure, that land ownership usually conveys buried items, and that the UK now requires finds of value or antiquity to be reported and pays market value to finders, unlike older finders keepers rules. They also describe UK and US reporting and waiting periods for found cash.

segments.title: Lost, mislaid, and abandoned property
segments.summary: The hosts define the three categories of contemporary found property: lost, mislaid, and abandoned. Mislaid property is left somewhere intentionally and forgotten, such as cash left on a bank counter, and the property owner is expected to safeguard it.

segments.title: Arizona buried cash case
segments.summary: A man who died had hidden about half a million dollars in cans in the walls of a house. The new owners found it during renovations, and his daughters claimed it. The hosts discuss how buying property can include everything on it, and the Texas private property view, and they debate whether the finders should give the money back.

segments.title: Georgia public defender and the found diamond ring
segments.summary: In 2013 a Georgia public defender pocketed a diamond engagement ring found in a Target store. Target reviewed surveillance video and a warrant was issued for the public defender's arrest. The hosts recommend turning lost items into police and advertising them.
topics: what to do with found property

segments.title: Undersea shipwreck treasure law
segments.summary: Shipwreck treasure is more complicated than land finds because of ship origin, location in territorial or international waters, and competing claimants. The San Jose galleon off Colombia, claimed by Colombia, Spain, and Peru, is worth an estimated one to twelve billion dollars. The UNESCO convention offers best practices but is not binding law.

segments.title: Notre Dame de Deliverance, Abandoned Shipwreck Act, and Tommy Thompson
segments.summary: The Notre Dame de Deliverance, sunk off Florida in 1755 and found in 2002 by a US salvage company, is partly in international waters and partly in a national marine sanctuary, with Spain and France claiming it. The Abandoned Shipwreck Act gives US states title to wrecks in state waters with conditions. Tommy Thompson, who found the S.S. Central America, was jailed in Ohio for refusing to say where gold coins went.

segments.title: Listener mail on the Stanford prison experiment
segments.summary: A cognitive psychologist writes that the hosts' Stanford prison experiment episode helped in teaching, and raises the idea that the study's publicity may have shaped the Abu Ghraib abuses.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank the listener and give contact information for the show.
